newsitem.title: USA: Dollar/mark jumps at U.S. open after jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark jumps at U.S. open after jobs data.

text.p: The dollar opened firmer, then soared briefly above 1.74 marks as currency traders compared a report showing strength in the U.S. jobs market to an earlier news release pointing to weakness in the German employment picture, experts said.

The U.S. economy added 138,000 non-farm jobs in May, a figure well below the 219,000 gain expected on average by economists. However, non-farm payrolls in April were revised sharply higher to 323,000 from a previously reported 142,000.
Furthermore, the U.S. jobless rate unexpectedly fell to 4.8 percent in May, its lowest level since October 1973.
Economists polled by Reuters, on average, had expected the May jobless rate to inch up to 5.0 percent from 4.9 percent in April.
The Labor Department also reported that average hourly earnings increased to $12.19 in May from $12.15 in April. The April figure was revised from an originally reported $12.14.
Ruesch International market analyst Brian McCarthy noted that the market focused on the revision in payrolls from the previous month and the wage component.
"On balance, it does strengthen the case for a Federal Reserve hike," he added.
McCarthy also noted that there is a "clear contrast" between the U.S. employment report and the German jobs figures released earlier.

The dollar climbed to 1.7375/85 marks at the open from 1.7275/80 at Thursday's close. Shortly after the U.S. employment numbers hit the market, the greenback jumped to 1.7423 marks, its highest level in 39 months.
Against the yen, the dollar rose to 115.86/91 from 115.60/70. After the jobs data, it briefly poked above 116.
But profit-taking emerged after the dollar soared, according to dealers.
This left the U.S. currency trading below 1.74 marks as the morning progressed.
Hypobank vice president Richard Vullo said: "We got the move up. We took out some stops and then...a lot of the selling was coming out of Europe."
Vullo noted that market players in both Europe and the U.S. went "long" dollar/mark ahead of the release of the U.S. employment report.
Initially, dollar/mark had gained after German jobless data came across the news wires, some experts said.
German unemployment rose a seasonally adjusted 56,000 to 4.358 million in May and the jobless rate crept up to 11.4 percent in May from 11.2 percent in April.
In the wake of the two key reports released on Friday, experts contrasted the outlook for interest rates in Germany and the U.S.

"What it means for Germany, I think, is that the Bundesbank is not going to be in any hurry to raise rates because of the weakness in the economy," said Diego Giurleo, a vice president of Treasury at Royal Bank of Canada.
"And the result of that is this interest rate advantage that the dollar has will be maintained," Giurleo added.

Following the release of the German figures, Federal Labor Office President Bernhard Jagoda said he could no longer endorse the government's official forecast of 3.95 million average unemployment in 1997. Another Labor Office official said that average unemployment could go as high as 4.29 million, based on data from the first five months of the year and an assumption of 2.25 percent economic growth.
The mark was also pressured by these remarks, according to some experts.
Turning to developments in Britain, the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee hiked official rates to 6.50 percent from 6.25 percent after its first meeting on Friday.
Yet the pound registered little reaction to the tightening.
Giurleo contended the market is still trying to digest a comment made earlier this week by Bank of England Governor Eddie George.

George had told reporters that the immediate problem is to balance the degree of tension between the pressure of domestic demand, which has been running a bit above a sustainable rate, with the exaggerated strength of the exchange rate.
"That's what took the steam out of sterling and, I think, that's still taking the steam out of it," Giurleo said.
Sterling fell to $1.6215/25 from $1.6340/50.
The dollar rose to 1.4595/05 Swiss francs from 1.4462/72 francs, and climbed to Canadian $1.3795/00 from C$1.3765/70.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7606/11, down from $0.7611/16 at the previous close.
